analysis.one_liner: Blocks credit bureaus from reporting medical debt tied to COVID-19 illness for lower-income people.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in March 2020 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that debt arising from a COVID-19 related illness could not appear as negative information on a person's credit report. It applied to people earning under $50,000 a year, or married couples filing jointly earning under $75,000. Protection was limited in time: it covered debt incurred within one year of the bill's passage, and only if the credit bureau knew the debt came from a COVID-19 illness. The bill was introduced on March 27, 2020, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never advanced further [S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Lower- and middle-income people who got sick with COVID-19 and fell behind on bills. Without protection, unpaid medical bills and other debt tied to the illness would show up on credit reports, lowering credit scores and making it harder and more expensive to rent an apartment, buy a car, or get a loan. The bill would have shielded that debt from credit reports for those earning under $50,000 (or $75,000 for married couples filing jointly) [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would have barred consumer reporting agencies from putting any adverse information about COVID-19 illness-related debt on a consumer's credit report [S2][S3].
Protection was targeted to individuals earning less than $50,000 a year, or married couples filing jointly earning less than $75,000 [S2][S3].
It covered debt incurred within one year of enactment, limiting the shield to the immediate pandemic period [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies and debt collectors. The three big bureaus would have been required to screen out known COVID-related medical debt rather than report it, and collection agencies and creditors would have lost the leverage of a damaged credit score when pursuing these debts [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill required the credit bureau to have actual knowledge that a debt arose from a COVID-19 related illness; hospitals and collectors do not systematically flag medical debts by diagnosis, so many sick borrowers would never have gotten the protection [S3].
It did not forgive or reduce any debt — people would still owe the money and could still be sued or sent to collections; only the credit report entry was blocked [S2][S3].
Shielding credit reports from medical debt can raise costs for other borrowers if lenders price in the unreported risk, though the one-year and income limits kept the scope narrow [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea was sound for the moment — people hospitalized with a novel disease in 2020 were not delinquent by choice, and a wrecked credit score compounds a health crisis. But the design was weak: it protected only the credit report, not the debt itself, and its 'actual knowledge' requirement made it hard to enforce in practice. Still, the cost to the credit bureaus was small relative to the benefit to sick low-income borrowers, and a fair hearing would have let Congress weigh fixes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee in late March 2020, and the committee never took it up; it sat there until the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Murphy introduced the bill in the House on March 27, 2020 [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, the committee with jurisdiction over the Fair Credit Reporting Act [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies and debt collectors are better off: nothing changed, so COVID-related debt continued to hit credit reports with full collection leverage intact. Sick borrowers got no relief from this bill.

for.name: Greg Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee; took no further recorded steps on it.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 27, 2020 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: With no cosponsors, no hearings, and no votes, the record shows no partisan positions taken on the bill either way [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have barred the bureaus from reporting known COVID-illness-related debt for lower-income people, cutting off a flow of adverse data that feeds their scoring business. The bill died, so nothing changed for them [S2][S3].
Collectors rely on credit reporting as leverage to push people to pay old debts. Shielding COVID medical debt from reports would have weakened that leverage for this class of debts [S3].
